segments.en: Listen to the Pacific breaking on a coral reef, all the way around you. On Nauru you are never far from that sound, because this is one small, round island sitting just south of the equator, on its own in the middle of a very big ocean.

You could walk right around it in an afternoon. One road circles the whole coast, and locals like to say that if you keep driving, you will always end up back where you started, usually with a friend waving from the roadside.

Nauru is one of the smallest countries in the world, and it has no official capital city. Government offices and the parliament sit in the district of Yaren, on the southern shore, close to the airport runway that stretches beside the sea.
The people call themselves Nauruans, and they speak Nauruan, a language found nowhere else, as well as English. A friendly greeting you will hear is Ekamawir omo, which means good morning.

Family life here is built around twelve traditional tribes, and belonging to your mother's tribe is part of who you are. Every tribe has its own story, and the national flag carries a white star with twelve points, one for each of them.

Look inland and the land rises to a high central plateau called Topside. For much of the last century, phosphate was mined there, and what remains is a strange landscape of grey coral pinnacles, like a forest made of stone.
Down on the coast the island is green and gentle, with coconut palms, pandanus trees and a quiet lagoon called Buada, surrounded by gardens. It is a lovely spot to watch the evening light fade.

Fishing has always mattered. In old times Nauruans caught young milkfish and raised them in ponds, and people were also famous for taming frigatebirds, the great black seabirds that glide above the reef.

If you are invited to share a meal, you might taste fresh reef fish, coconut, breadfruit and rice, often cooked for a whole extended family. Food is shared generously, and nobody leaves a gathering hungry.

The biggest celebration is Angam Day, held each October. Angam means homecoming, and the day remembers times when the number of Nauruans grew back after hard years, a reminder of how precious every single person is.
Before you leave, sit on the reef edge at sunset and watch the sky turn orange over the water. Then follow the ocean north and east to Kiribati, a nation of islands spread across the Pacific.
